definition: Assimilation means the process of being absorbed into a larger group or culture.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word assimilation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know assimilation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Linguists date the loanword's full assimilation to the 1960s, when English printers quietly stopped setting it in italics.
Acceptance means the group lets you in and leaves you as you are; assimilation reaches deeper — the group's ways become your ways.
Integration is full membership with your own colors kept; assimilation goes further, blending you in until newcomer and native can't be told apart.

Absorption is being taken in by anything at all — a sponge absorbs water, a firm absorbs a rival, a crowd absorbs a stranger — with no cultural claim attached. Assimilation is absorption of one particular kind: a person or group taken into a larger culture until the seam stops showing.

Naturalization is the legal act of becoming a citizen — forms, a test, an oath, a certificate with a date on it. Assimilation is the slower cultural change no office can grant: taking on the larger group's ways until the difference fades. Many people are naturalized years before they are ever assimilated.

That erasing of the seam is assimilation.
Assimilation is the precise word because it names being absorbed into a larger group or culture — not visiting it, not copying it for a night.
Integration would leave the family recognizably mainland while taking full part; assimilation goes further, folding them in until the difference stops showing at all.
Assimilation is the social-science word for being absorbed into a larger group or culture, and it can carry real weight — gain and loss at once — so use it where that depth belongs.

If the newcomers keep their own identity while taking full part, the honest word is integration, not assimilation.

My grandmother's citizenship certificate is dated 1952, three years after she landed; she framed it and hung it in the hall.
Her assimilation took far longer, and no office ever issued a paper for it.
It happened in small installments: the recipes she swapped with neighbors, the ballgames she learned to argue about, the accent that softened until strangers stopped asking where she was from.
By the time I knew her, her sentences ran on the same rhythms as everyone else's on the street.
The certificate made her a citizen in an afternoon; becoming indistinguishable from her neighbors was the work of thirty years.
